title: Nankana Sahib

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj, two places in Delhi for one death, and two ordinary men who did the carrying. Your line was where he gave his head. Where did you take three slow breaths? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

Some families keep a map of a child's first years without ever drawing one. That's the bench where she learned to ride a bike. That's the corner shop where he spent his first coin. That's the field where the dog ran off. Point at a street and someone says, that's where it happened. Now take that habit and give it to a whole people, about one boy, in one small town in Punjab. The town was called Talwandi. Today it's called Nankana Sahib, and its streets are a family map of a childhood.
screen: `A MAP OF A CHILD'S FIRST YEARS.` → `THAT'S WHERE IT HAPPENED.` → `ONE TOWN, ONE BOY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition says Guru Nanak was born in the village of Talwandi, and the town later came to be called Nankana Sahib, after him. Today it sits in Pakistan, as this path has told before. Second, the map. Sikh tradition marks the boy's story place by place. Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the birthplace, stands where tradition says the house was. Nearby, other gurdwaras keep other stories. One marks where the boy played with other children. One, Patti Sahib, marks the school where tradition says he learned his letters and surprised his teacher with what he did with them. One marks the field where the cattle he was minding wandered into a neighbor's crop, and, in the story, the crop was found unharmed. One marks the tree where, in the story, a cobra spread its hood to shade him as he slept. Year one told those stories. Here, they have addresses. Third, how to hold a map like that. These places rest on the janamsakhis, the life-stories, and Sikhs read them in different ways: some as plain history, some as loving pictures of who Nanak was. Either way, the map says something true about how Sikhs remember him. Not as a figure who appeared fully grown, but as a boy who played, went to school, minded cattle, fell asleep in a field. Fourth, the light. The poet Bhai Gurdas describes the moment Guru Nanak came into the world, here in paraphrase: when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world. That's the big picture. Nankana Sahib is the small one: a town where you can stand on the spot and say, it began here. That's today's line: where it began.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the village. Settle, and breathe. See a small town on the Punjab plain, flat fields, a few trees, low houses. See a boy running between them. A school with slates. A field with cattle. A tree with deep shade. Let it be ordinary. Then, without hurrying, bring to mind the place where your own story began, a house, a street, a hospital, a town. Rest in both pictures for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Nankana Sahib. The town once called Talwandi, where tradition says Guru Nanak was born, with gurdwaras marking the stories of his childhood. Today's word.
Your line: where it began. Today, tell someone one small true story from the place you grew up, and name the exact spot where it happened. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims cross into Pakistan to visit Nankana Sahib, especially for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary, and go from gurdwara to gurdwara, each marking a story from his childhood.
